description: activerecord's classification against the conformance corpus (conformance/actions.json). 'adapterUnsupported' lists 'conformance' actions this adapter cannot express, each with the reason (naming the real mechanism) and the substring its thrown error must contain. 'adapterSupportedExpected' lists 'expectedUnsupported' actions this adapter deliberately translates, so they are oracle-compared instead of thrown. 'expectedUnsupportedMessages' pins the throw message for every 'expectedUnsupported' action it does not promote, and 'nullRepresentationOmittedMessages' for every 'nullRepresentationOmitted' action. validate-corpus.sh checks all four against the corpus; the harness refuses to run with a message missing.

adapterUnsupported.message: int() applied to a :string column: CEL reads the WHOLE string or makes an error, and Cerbos then denies the row, but SQL reads the digits at the front and gives a number, so the filter would keep the row. Compare the column directly, or give an operator override.

adapterUnsupported.reason: The mapper supplies a string column; the adapter only compares instants through native temporal columns, without portable error-preserving parsing of malformed strings.

adapterUnsupported.reason: The planner folds `now() - duration("24h")` to a literal with nanosecond precision, and ActiveRecord binds a Time into SQL at microsecond precision at best — SQLite stores a formatted string and MySQL DATETIME(6) truncates. Rounding the literal compares against a different instant than the policy names, in the direction that admits rows just outside the window, so the adapter refuses rather than move the boundary
adapterUnsupported.message: carries sub-microsecond precision, which ActiveRecord truncates when binding a Time into SQL

adapterUnsupported.reason: The same sub-microsecond now() literal as ts-window, reached with the operands the other way round. Operand order does not change what a Time binds as, so the refusal is the same one
adapterUnsupported.message: carries sub-microsecond precision, which ActiveRecord truncates when binding a Time into SQL

adapterUnsupported.reason: The denominator is a DIFFERENT column, so it may be zero on a row where the numerator is not. CEL divides to a signed Infinity and IEEE-754 keeps the sign of the zero; SQL cannot tell -0.0 from 0.0, and a NULLIF guard collapses both to NULL. The sign of the Infinity decides which side of an order comparison the row falls on, so no guard recovers it and the adapter refuses. A constant denominator, or a column divided by itself, stays translatable
adapterUnsupported.message: Cannot divide by a column that may be zero

adapterUnsupported.reason: CEL carries a NaN or a signed Infinity out of the division and through the arithmetic composed on top of it; SQL has no value that does, because the NULLIF divide-by-zero guard turns the whole sum into NULL. The adapter resolves a non-finite division only where the division IS the comparison operand, so a division nested under further arithmetic fails closed instead of emitting the under-granting filter
adapterUnsupported.message: add cannot take an operand that may be NaN or Infinity

adapterUnsupported.reason: The same nested-division limitation as cr-div-then-add, and the arm that proves it matters: `NaN != 2.0` is TRUE and the PDP allows the zero row, while `NULL + 1 <> 2` is UNKNOWN and drops it
adapterUnsupported.message: add cannot take an operand that may be NaN or Infinity

adapterUnsupported.reason: Positional access into a scalar list. `index` has no case in the translator's operator dispatch at all, so the walk falls through to the generic unsupported-operator refusal rather than to a leaf-operand guard — which is why the message names the operator and offers an override. No case was written because row order in a SQL relation is not defined without an ORDER BY the plan does not carry: `tagNames` is a has_many association, and `tagNames[0]` names whichever row the engine happens to return first. A caller whose table has a deterministic ordering column can express it faithfully, and the override the message offers is that escape hatch

adapterUnsupported.reason: The cross-type probe `aBoolList[0] == 1 || aNumber == 5`, refused at the `index` in its first disjunct for the same missing element order as index-bool-list, so nothing is emitted for either disjunct. The refusal is also what keeps the cross-type hazard shut on this store: SQLite holds a boolean column as the integer 1, so a positional lowering that compared the stored `aBoolList` element with the literal would return b4 and c1, whose first element is true, where CEL's heterogeneous equality is false for every row
adapterUnsupported.message: Unsupported operator: index. Supply an operator override if the database can express it faithfully.

The refusal is also what keeps the cross-type hazard shut on this store: SQLite reads the literal TRUE as the integer 1, so a positional lowering that compared the stored `aNumberList` element with the literal would return b4, whose first element is 1, where CEL's heterogeneous equality is false for every row

adapterUnsupported.reason: map() is held as a projected relation until size() or hasIntersection() gives it a scalar meaning as an aggregate or an EXISTS subquery. Comparing the ordered projection itself to a literal list gives it neither, and a correlated subquery has no ordering to compare element-wise against, so the held projection reaches a plain value position and is refused there
adapterUnsupported.message: eq cannot take a collection operand (a projected relation)

adapterUnsupported.reason: An empty delimiter is refused when the hierarchy operand is parsed, before the descendant LIKE is built: the adapter emits `prefix + delimiter + '%'`, which with an empty delimiter is a bare string-prefix LIKE that also matches the path itself (a2, never its own descendant)
adapterUnsupported.message: hierarchy() delimiter must be a non-empty string
